item.title: Theker Raises $85M for Factory Robots That Don't Specialize
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Barcelona startup closed what it calls Europe's largest robotics Series A to build AI-native factory robots that deploy in days and keep learning on the line.
item.content:encoded:
Theker, a four-year-old Barcelona startup, has raised $85 million (about €73 million) to build factory robots that aren't built for any one task. The company calls it the largest robotics Series A ever in Europe, and the investor list backs up the ambition.

CRV led the round, with Samsung, LVMH, Cathay Innovation, 20VC, Henkel Ventures, Korelya, and Bright Pixel Capital joining. A few of those are firsts: Samsung's first investment in a Spanish company, LVMH's first bet on a Spanish startup, and CRV's first deal in Spain. When a luxury house and a chip-and-appliance giant write checks into the same industrial-robotics round, the pitch is landing across very different factory floors.

Theker was founded in 2022 by Jiaqiang Ye Zhu and Carla Gomez Cano, and its argument is a direct shot at how industrial robots have worked for decades. Traditional arms are rigid and task-specific, expensive to reprogram every time a production line changes. Theker's pitch is AI-native generalist robots that deploy in days and keep learning while they run, adapting to the messiness of a real plant instead of demanding the plant adapt to them.

That's also the claim to watch. "Generalist robot that learns on the job" is the line half the robotics and humanoid field is selling right now, and the demo always looks great. The proof is whether tier-one industrial operators run these things in production at scale, not in a staged cell. Theker says the money goes toward exactly that: more deployments with large operators, deeper work on its own AI and robotics stack, and hiring across software, electronics, mechanical engineering, and field deployment.

Either way, an $85 million Series A out of Barcelona is a real signal about where serious robotics money is going, and that it isn't all flowing to the usual hubs in the US and China.

item.title: Anthropic Passes OpenAI in US Business AI Adoption, Ramp Data Shows
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Ramp's spend-based index puts Anthropic at roughly 41% of US businesses with paid AI subscriptions in June, ahead of an OpenAI that has gone flat.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, more US businesses are paying Anthropic than OpenAI. That's the headline from the Ramp AI Index, and the June reading widens a gap that first appeared in April.

The numbers: Anthropic reached about 41% of US businesses with paid AI subscriptions in June, while OpenAI held roughly flat. The crossover happened in April, when Anthropic climbed to 34.4% and OpenAI slipped to 32.3%. Pull back further and the trajectory is the real story. Anthropic sat at 0.03% of businesses in mid-2023, reached 7.94% by April 2025, and then more than quadrupled over the following year.

What makes this worth more than the usual adoption press release is where the data comes from. The Ramp AI Index is built on actual corporate-card and invoice payments flowing through Ramp's customer base, not a survey asking executives which model they like. Real dollars are harder to fake than sentiment.

They're also narrower than they look. This measures the share of businesses with a paid subscription, not revenue, not seat counts, not consumer usage where OpenAI still dominates. Ramp's customer base skews toward startups and smaller companies, exactly the buyers who adopt developer-friendly tools first, so the index reads as a leading indicator more than a full market census. A win on "number of businesses paying" is real, but it isn't the same as a win on money.

VentureBeat noted three threats that could erase the lead, and the caution is fair: pricing pressure, a strong model release from a competitor, and enterprise procurement cycles that move slowly can all reverse a trend built largely on early adopters. For now, though, the company that spent years as the safety-focused underdog is the one businesses are putting on the card.

item.title: A Langflow Path-Traversal Bug Is Under Attack on Exposed AI Servers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-5027 lets attackers write files anywhere on a Langflow host through an unsanitized upload endpoint, and researchers have tied the activity to Iran's MuddyWater.
item.content:encoded:
Roughly 7,000 Langflow instances sit exposed on the public internet, most of them in North America, and attackers are working through them. CVE-2026-5027 is a path-traversal flaw in the popular open-source AI workflow builder, and it's being exploited in the wild.

The mechanics are mundane in the way the worst bugs often are. The POST /api/v2/files endpoint doesn't sanitize the filename it receives in multipart form data, so an attacker can stuff ../ sequences into that field and write files wherever they want on the host. Arbitrary file write is rarely the end goal; it's the on-ramp. From there you get remote code execution, persistence, credential theft, and the ability to quietly rewrite the AI workflows the platform exists to run. The flaw rates 8.8.

Threat intelligence has linked the exploitation to MuddyWater, a group assessed to operate on behalf of Iran. Treat that attribution as the analysts present it, with confidence but not certainty. The more useful takeaway is who's bothering: when a state-aligned crew starts sweeping a specific tool, it means that tool has become infrastructure worth targeting, and AI development platforms are now squarely in that bucket.

Langflow has shipped a fix in version 1.10.0, but exploitation was already running before broad patching, which is the recurring pattern with anything internet-facing and convenient to stand up. Plenty of those 7,000 instances were spun up fast by developers who never meant to leave them reachable.

If you run Langflow, upgrade to 1.10.0 now, and the harder question is whether it should be on the open internet at all. Put it behind authentication and a VPN or reverse proxy, check the host for files that shouldn't be there, and assume an exposed-and-unpatched instance may already be compromised.

item.title: Cisco SD-WAN Manager Bug Is Being Exploited and Has No Patch Yet
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-20245, a root-level command injection flaw in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, to its exploited-vulnerabilities catalog while a dedicated fix is still pending.
item.content:encoded:
Cisco's Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, the console that pushes configuration to entire SD-WAN fabrics, has a command injection flaw that attackers are already using. CISA added CVE-2026-20245 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 9, and as of that listing there was no dedicated patch.

The bug rates 7.8 on CVSS, which undersells it. It stems from insufficient validation of user-supplied input in the CLI, and it lets an attacker run arbitrary commands as root. The product, formerly known as vManage, is affected across On-Prem, Cloud-Pro, Cloud Managed, and FedRAMP deployments. Cisco describes the observed activity as limited, with some cases resulting in configuration changes pushed down to edge devices.

That last detail is the whole story. A 7.8 that requires an authenticated foothold sounds like a contained problem until you remember what this box does. Root on the controller that programs every branch router is the kind of access that turns one compromised account into quiet control over the network it manages. Config changes to edge devices are not a side effect; they're the payoff.

Google Mandiant researchers Chester Sng, Pete Boonyakarn, and Logeswaran Nadarajan found and reported the flaw. Cisco's interim guidance points operators to the releases that addressed an earlier vManage bug, CVE-2026-20182, which shipped on May 14, and to watch /var/log/scripts.log for signs of exploitation.

If you run SD-WAN Manager, restrict access to the management plane to known administrators, get on the May releases if you aren't already, and start hunting in scripts.log now rather than after the dedicated fix lands. A KEV entry with no patch is CISA telling you the clock started before the vendor finished.

item.title: Splunk Patches a 9.8 Pre-Auth RCE Hiding in Its Postgres Sidecar
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-20253 lets an unauthenticated attacker create or overwrite files on a Splunk Enterprise host through an unprotected PostgreSQL endpoint, and from there reach code execution.
item.content:encoded:
One HTTP request to the right endpoint, no credentials required, and an attacker can create or truncate files on a Splunk Enterprise box. That is the heart of CVE-2026-20253, and it sits inside a product whose entire job is to watch everything else for signs of trouble.

The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8. It lives in a PostgreSQL sidecar service that ships with Splunk Enterprise, exposing two HTTP endpoints (/v1/postgres/recovery/backup and /v1/postgres/recovery/restore) with no authentication in front of them. Those endpoints were meant to be internal, but Splunk's main web application proxies through to them, which puts the whole thing one reachable hop from the internet. An attacker who can write arbitrary files on the host has a short, well-worn path to remote code execution.

Who's exposed depends on how you run it. The sidecar was introduced in version 10, so anything on the 10.x line and up is in scope. Researchers at Orca Security, who reported the chain, flagged AWS-hosted deployments as the worst case because the sidecar is installed and enabled by default there. On-prem Windows installs are less immediately exposed since the service often isn't installed or running, but "less exposed" is not "safe," and you should confirm rather than assume.

Splunk disclosed this alongside three other high-severity bugs and shipped fixes in 10.4.0, 10.2.4, and 10.0.7. The upgrade math is simple: 10.0.0 through 10.0.6 land on 10.0.7, and 10.2.0 through 10.2.3 land on 10.2.4.

There's a particular irony in a SIEM platform being the unauthenticated entry point, and it's worth sitting with. Security tooling tends to run with broad access to logs, credentials, and the rest of the estate, which makes it a high-value target precisely because it's trusted. A pre-auth file write here isn't just one server; it's a server that can see a lot of others.

If you operate Splunk Enterprise on 10.x, upgrade now, and treat any internet-reachable instance as a priority. Check whether the PostgreSQL sidecar is enabled, restrict access to the management interfaces, and review your hosts for unexpected files or processes that predate the patch.

item.title: SpaceX Pops 19% on Its First Day, and MSCI Is Already Adding It
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SpaceX closed its first day on the Nasdaq up 19% at $160.95, and as of June 13 MSCI's early-inclusion rules pull SPCX into its large-cap indexes barely a day after the record $75 billion IPO.
item.content:encoded:
$160.95. That is where SpaceX closed its first day as a public company, up about 19 percent from a $135 IPO price, trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker SPCX.

The mechanics behind that number are staggering even by recent standards. SpaceX sold roughly 555.6 million shares and raised around $75 billion, the largest initial public offering on record. The stock opened near $150, ran past a 30 percent gain at one intraday point, and briefly carried a valuation above $2.2 trillion. On paper, the debut also made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.

The reason this is news on June 13 rather than just yesterday's pop is MSCI. Under its early-inclusion methodology, MSCI adds a newly listed company of this size to its large-cap indexes almost immediately, a day after listing rather than waiting for the usual quarterly review. That forces every fund tracking those indexes to buy SPCX whether they have a view on it or not.

Which is the part worth sitting with. A 19 percent first-day jump is usually read as a triumph, but it also means the offering was priced below what the market would bear, and the company left money on the table that went to first-day buyers instead. And index inclusion is mechanical demand, not a judgment on the business. Passive funds are buying because the rules say to, not because anyone ran the numbers on a launch company whose cash flows are lumpy and whose capital appetite is enormous.

What justifies a two-trillion-dollar tag is not the IPO mechanics. It is Starship cadence and Starlink revenue, the two lines that have to keep climbing for this valuation to look like anything other than enthusiasm. The stock now trades on both, in public, every day. That is the actual change here.

item.title: France's Sovereign Messenger Tchap Breached, 73,000 Accounts Exposed
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A hijacked account led to a breach of Tchap, France's Matrix-based government messenger, exposing data tied to 73,000 public-sector users and more than 640,000 messages.
item.content:encoded:
Tchap was France's answer to depending on foreign chat apps for government work. This week it got breached.

French authorities confirmed a security incident dated June 7, and the agency that runs the platform, DINUM, says fewer than 9 percent of registered users were affected. The attacker tells a bigger story: claims of 73,000 exposed accounts, more than 640,000 messages, and roughly 13.5GB of documents and media exfiltrated. The entry point was not some exotic exploit. It was social engineering against a single user account, after which the attacker says they reached hardcoded LDAP credentials and pulled data from there.

What got exposed, by the official account, came from public discussions: usernames, email addresses, profile images, and the government organizations users belong to. Private chats are said to have stayed protected, since Tchap runs on the end-to-end encrypted Matrix protocol. Investigators are still reviewing exactly what the attacker could reach, which is the polite way of saying the "private chats are safe" line is provisional.

There is an irony here that is hard to ignore. Tchap launched in 2018 as a joint project of DINUM and the national cybersecurity agency ANSSI, built on Matrix specifically so that French public-sector communications would not run through American or other foreign platforms. It is a sovereignty project, and it was undone by a hijacked account and credentials hardcoded somewhere they should never have been.

Even granting that message bodies held, the metadata alone matters for a government. Who works at which ministry, who talks to whom, which email maps to which official: that is exactly the kind of mapping a foreign intelligence service would pay for. The encryption did its job on content. The breach still handed over the shape of the organization.

item.title: A Fake Error Report Can Make Your Coding Agent Run Malicious Code
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Tenet Security's 'Agentjacking' shows how a poisoned Sentry error event can trick Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex into running attacker-supplied commands, with an 85% success rate in testing.
item.content:encoded:
The error report your AI agent reads to fix a bug can be the attack. That is the uncomfortable idea behind Agentjacking, a technique published this week by Tenet Security.

Here is the mechanism. Sentry is the error-tracking tool a huge number of teams already run, and it now exposes an MCP server so coding agents can pull error details and propose fixes. Tenet found that an attacker can inject crafted text into a Sentry error event, and when the agent reads that event through the MCP server, it cannot tell the attacker's instructions apart from Sentry's own remediation guidance. The agent treats the injected commands as a legitimate next step and runs them. It is indirect prompt injection, weaponized through a tool developers already trust.

The numbers are the part that should bother you. Tenet says it hijacked Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex with an 85 percent success rate in controlled tests, and it identified 2,388 exposed organizations, ranging from a company worth a quarter-trillion dollars down to solo developers and, awkwardly, a cloud-security vendor.

The detail that breaks the usual reassurances: the agents ran the attacker's code even when explicitly told to ignore it, and endpoint detection, firewalls, and prompt-level guardrails all missed it. The standard mitigation story for prompt injection has been some version of "instruct the model not to comply," and this is a clean demonstration that the instruction does not hold when the malicious input arrives dressed as trusted tool output.

This is the structural tension in agentic tooling. The autonomy that lets an agent read your errors and fix them is the same autonomy that lets injected instructions act on your machine, and every MCP connection widens the set of places that poison can come from. Treating tool output as trusted is the bug, and right now most setups do exactly that.

If you run coding agents against real systems, scope their permissions hard, sandbox anything they execute, and stop letting them auto-run proposed commands against production. The safe default is to treat everything an agent reads from an external source as untrusted input, including the error reports it was built to help with.

item.title: Police Seize AudiA6, the Mixer That Washed $380M for Ransomware Crews
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: An international operation led by Europol and the US DOJ dismantled AudiA6, a crypto-laundering service that cleaned more than $380 million for ransomware gangs and arrested two of its alleged operators in Georgia.
item.content:encoded:
A service that promised to launder dirty cryptocurrency and return it clean in about an hour, for a cut of 3 to 10 percent, is offline. Two of its alleged operators are now in custody in Georgia.

The takedown of AudiA6 came on June 10, run jointly by the US Department of Justice, the Secret Service, and Europol. Investigators say the platform operated as a central laundering hub from 2022 to 2025 and moved more than $380 million, roughly 336 million euros, for criminal clients. The coordinated action seized 25 domains, pulled more than 30 servers offline, confiscated over 80 vehicles and several properties in Georgia, and froze around 692,000 euros in crypto. The two administrators arrested hold Ukrainian and Russian nationality.

Ransomware gets the headlines, but cashing out is the part that actually constrains it. Encrypting a hospital is easy. Turning the ransom into spendable money without getting traced is the hard problem, and services like AudiA6 are the plumbing that solves it. Europol says the operation has been linked to more than 15 separate ransomware investigations, which is the real measure of what just got disrupted.

Worth being clear-eyed about what this does and does not accomplish. Domain seizures are reversible, and mixer operators rebrand and resurface with depressing regularity. What raises the cost is the arrests and the asset seizures, the part where running this business stops being anonymous and starts being a prison sentence. That is the difference between knocking over a storefront and actually deterring the trade.

For defenders, the takeaway is less about any single service and more about the pressure on the cash-out layer. Every laundering pipeline that gets dismantled makes the economics of ransomware a little worse, which is slow, unglamorous progress, and the only kind that lasts.

item.title: Google Patches a Chrome V8 Zero-Day That's Already Being Exploited
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Chrome 149.0.7827.102 fixes CVE-2026-11645, an actively exploited out-of-bounds bug in the V8 engine that lets a malicious web page run code inside the browser sandbox.
item.content:encoded:
Every Chrome user has an update waiting, and this one is not optional. Google pushed a fix on June 8 for CVE-2026-11645, a flaw in V8 that attackers are already using against real targets.

V8 is the engine that runs JavaScript and WebAssembly on every page Chrome loads, which is what makes a bug here serious. This one is an out-of-bounds memory access rated 8.8, and a crafted HTML page is enough to trigger code execution inside the browser sandbox. A user does not have to download anything. Visiting the wrong page is the whole exploit.

The flaw was reported on April 27 by a researcher credited as 303f06e3, who collected a $55,000 bounty for it. That leaves a gap of roughly six weeks between the report and the public fix, which is normal for a complex engine bug but worth noticing given that exploitation was happening in that window. The patch ships in Chrome 149.0.7827.102 and .103 for Windows and macOS, and .102 for Linux.

Google is holding back the technical detail on the exploit until most users have updated, which is standard practice and also a tell that the bug is being used in ways the team does not want to advertise. A sandbox-contained flaw is not full system compromise on its own, but these rarely travel alone. They get chained with a sandbox escape, and then it is a different conversation. CISA added the CVE to its exploited-vulnerabilities catalog on June 9.

The action here is boring and immediate. Open your version page, confirm you are on 149.0.7827.102 or later, and restart the browser to apply it. If you manage a fleet, push the update through policy rather than trusting users to relaunch on their own.

item.title: Check Point VPN Zero-Day Under Attack Since May, Now in CISA's KEV
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-50751, a 9.3-rated authentication bypass in Check Point's Remote Access VPN, has been exploited since early May, with at least one intrusion tied to a Qilin ransomware affiliate.
item.content:encoded:
An attacker can open a VPN session into a Check Point gateway without a valid password. That is the whole problem with CVE-2026-50751, and it has been happening in the wild since May 7.

The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.3 and is classified as improper authentication. It lives in the IKEv1 key-exchange logic, and it lets an unauthenticated attacker establish a session as though they had legitimate credentials. It affects Remote Access VPN, Mobile Access, and the Spark Firewall line across nine version branches, from R80.20.x up through R82.10. If you run a Check Point gateway exposed to the internet, the odds are good you are in scope.

Rapid7's researchers confirmed two intrusions with high confidence and tied at least one of them, with medium confidence, to an affiliate of the Qilin ransomware operation. Check Point's own framing calls the campaign limited, several dozen organizations so far. That number is doing a lot of work. A perimeter VPN that hands out authenticated sessions is exactly the front door a ransomware crew wants, and "several dozen" is a snapshot, not a ceiling. Once a reliable exploit circulates, limited campaigns stop being limited.

Check Point has shipped hotfixes, and CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in early June with a federal remediation deadline attached. That KEV listing is the part defenders should read as a clock, not a footnote: it means the government has seen enough real exploitation to compel agencies to patch.

If you operate these gateways, apply the hotfix now and treat any internet-facing instance as potentially already touched. Hunt for VPN sessions you cannot account for, new or unexpected administrative activity, and the usual post-access tradecraft that precedes a ransomware deployment. Patching closes the door. It does not tell you whether someone already walked through it.

item.title: KKR and Nvidia Put $10B Into a Company to Fix Stalled AI Data Centers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: KKR, Nvidia, Vistra, and Kuwait's sovereign fund launched Helix Digital Infrastructure with more than $10 billion to build the power and data centers hyperscalers keep announcing but failing to deliver.
item.content:encoded:
There's a gap between the data centers companies announce and the ones that actually come online. KKR just put more than $10 billion behind closing it.

On June 11, KKR, Nvidia, Vistra, and the Kuwait Investment Authority launched Helix Digital Infrastructure, a company built to finance and deliver AI infrastructure for hyperscale customers. The pitch is integration: bundle data center capacity, power, connectivity, and the services around them into one package, instead of making a hyperscaler stitch those pieces together itself. Nvidia comes in as the strategic technology partner, and Vistra as the preferred power supplier.

Running it is Adam Selipsky, who used to be CEO of Amazon Web Services. He isn't pretending the buildout is going smoothly. By his account, more than a quarter of announced data center projects aren't getting delivered, and Helix exists to attack that delivery gap rather than to add another splashy capacity number to the pile.

Selipsky's point about undelivered projects is the honest part of an otherwise familiar story. The constraint on AI infrastructure stopped being chips a while ago and became power, permits, and the ability to actually finish construction. Money keeps pouring in regardless. KKR's $10 billion lands the same week Amazon reportedly lined up $17.5 billion in bank loans and Google signed a compute deal with SpaceX worth about $920 million a month. A lot of capital is chasing the same scarce megawatts.

For everyone who isn't a hyperscaler, this is the plumbing of the AI boom getting financialized. Whether Helix delivers faster than the projects Selipsky is criticizing is the thing to watch. The capital is clearly available. Turning it into powered, online racks is the part that keeps slipping.

item.title: Is Security+ Worth It in 2026? An Honest Look at the SY0-701
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Security+ is the most-requested entry cybersecurity cert and a DoD baseline requirement, but it opens doors rather than handing you a six-figure analyst salary on day one.
item.content:encoded:
Security+ is the cert that gets oversold in both directions. One camp treats it as a golden ticket into a $125,000 security analyst job. The other dismisses it as a memorization test that proves nothing. Both are wrong, and the truth in between is genuinely good news: Security+ is the single most reliable way to get past a hiring filter for an entry-level security role, and that's a meaningful thing to buy for a few hundred dollars.

The current exam is SY0-701, and it's been the only active version since CompTIA retired SY0-601 in July 2024. It runs up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, including performance-based questions, and you need 750 out of 900 to pass. Retail pricing in the US sits around $425 for a single voucher. There's no formal prerequisite, though CompTIA suggests Network+ and a couple of years of IT experience first, and that background genuinely makes the exam easier.

The content is organized into five domains: General Security Concepts (12%), Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%), Security Architecture (18%), Security Operations (28%), and Security Program Management and Oversight (20%). The weighting toward operations and threats reflects what the cert is really for: showing you can function in a SOC or a security-adjacent IT role, not that you can write policy from scratch.

Now the salary question, handled honestly. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a 2024 median wage of $124,910 for information security analysts, with employment projected to grow 29% through 2034 and roughly 16,000 openings a year. That growth is real and it's why the cert is in demand. But that median reflects experienced analysts, not someone who just passed Security+. A fresh Security+ holder is typically looking at the bottom of that range or a notch below it, in roles like junior SOC analyst, security administrator, or an IT job with security duties. The cert points you up that ladder; it doesn't teleport you to the top of it.

There's one advantage that's easy to undersell: Security+ is an approved baseline certification under the US Department of Defense's workforce requirements (DoD 8140/8570). For a large set of government and defense-contractor roles, holding it isn't a nice-to-have, it's a checkbox you cannot be hired without. If that's the world you're aiming at, the worth-it question is already answered.

How hard is it? Moderate, and the difficulty is specific. The volume of terminology is large, and the performance-based questions reward people who've actually configured something over people who've only read about it. The other trap is CompTIA's question style, which loves asking for the "best" answer among several that are all defensible. Knowing the definition isn't enough; you have to know which control fits which scenario.

Which points at how to study. Professor Messer's free SY0-701 series remains the backbone most people build on, paired with a paid course if you want structure. But the candidates who pass on the first try are the ones who drill performance-based scenarios and run a question bank hard enough to expose the gap between "I recognize this term" and "I know when to use it." Hands-on practice and realistic question reps are what close that gap, far more than rereading a study guide. For an entry security cert in 2026, Security+ is worth it. Just buy it for what it is: the door, not the room.

item.title: Microsoft Built Its Own Frontier Models. The Target Is OpenAI's Bill.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft's seven new in-house MAI models, led by the reasoning model MAI-Thinking-1, are built to run on Azure without licensing fees, and the strategy matters more than the benchmarks.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft spent years reselling OpenAI's models as its own AI products. At Build this month it showed the alternative it's been building quietly: seven models trained in-house, headlined by MAI-Thinking-1, its first reasoning model.

MAI-Thinking-1 is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with about 35 billion active parameters out of roughly a trillion total, and a 256,000-token context window. Microsoft says it was trained on commercially licensed data with no distillation from third-party models, OpenAI's included. Alongside it: MAI-Code-1-Flash, a small 5-billion-parameter coding model headed into VS Code and GitHub Copilot, plus image, transcription, and voice models.

The benchmark line Microsoft is pushing is that in blind human comparisons MAI-Thinking-1 was preferred over Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6 and held its own against Claude Opus 4.6 on SWE Bench Pro coding tasks. Take that the way you take any vendor's own evals: directionally interesting, not independent proof. "Preferred in blind tests we ran" is a claim, not a leaderboard.

The benchmarks aren't the point anyway. The point is the bill. Every time Microsoft serves an OpenAI model, it pays for that model. Running its own models on Azure cuts the royalty out, and Satya Nadella framed the shift as moving from "consuming a frontier model to fully participating at the frontier." For developers, the promised payoff is lower per-token pricing. For Microsoft, it's options in a partnership that has grown lopsided, and room to negotiate the next OpenAI deal from a stronger position.

None of this means Microsoft is dropping OpenAI. GPT models still sit at the center of Copilot, and Microsoft has every reason to keep that relationship going. But a company that can credibly run its own frontier-class models is a different kind of partner than one that can't. That's the message Build was really sending.

item.title: Is the AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03) Worth It?
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The SAA-C03 is the most-requested cloud cert in job postings, but it rewards people who already know AWS and quietly punishes those treating it as a first step.
item.content:encoded:
The AWS Solutions Architect Associate is the cloud cert that shows up most in job postings, and that alone makes it worth taking seriously. But there's a trap baked into how people approach it. They see "associate" in the name and assume it's a beginner cert. It isn't. The SAA-C03 assumes you already understand how AWS services fit together, and it tests your judgment about which one to reach for, not whether you can define them.

The exam specifics: 65 questions in 130 minutes, of which 50 are scored and 15 are unscored items AWS uses to trial future questions. You need a scaled score of 720 out of 1,000 to pass, and it costs $150 in the US. There's no hard prerequisite, but AWS recommends about a year of hands-on experience, and that recommendation is doing more work than it looks.

Four domains, and the weighting tells the story: Design Secure Architectures (30%), Design Resilient Architectures (26%), Design High-Performing Architectures (24%), and Design Cost-Optimized Architectures (20%). Every domain is the word "design." That's the whole exam in one observation. You're not being asked what S3 is. You're being asked, given a scenario with latency targets, a budget, and a compliance constraint, which storage class and which architecture you'd choose. The questions are little case studies, often two or three plausible-looking answers deep.

That design framing is also why it's harder than the question count suggests. Two answers will usually be technically correct and one will be the right call for the scenario's actual priority, whether that's cost, durability, or recovery time. You can't pattern-match your way through that. You have to genuinely understand the tradeoffs between, say, Multi-AZ and read replicas, or when a NAT gateway beats a NAT instance. This is where pure flashcard study falls apart.

The payoff is real and it's the strongest of any cert in this group. The SAA shows up in a large share of cloud job listings, and aggregated salary data from sites like ZipRecruiter and Glassdoor puts cloud roles tied to it well into six figures, commonly in the $140,000-plus range for people with a couple of years of experience. Those are aggregator numbers rather than a government statistic, so read them as the shape of the market, not a guarantee. The direction is not in doubt: cloud architecture pays, and this cert is the recognized entry ticket.

Here's the honest catch for career-changers. If you have zero AWS exposure, going straight for the SAA is a slog, and many people would be better served starting with the Cloud Practitioner to build vocabulary first, then coming back. The fastest path through the SAA for anyone runs through the console: spin up the services the exam covers, break them, watch the bill, see what fails over and what doesn't. Pair that with scenario-style practice questions in the weeks before the exam, because the test's whole personality is scenarios, and reading documentation does not prepare you for the judgment calls the way actually building does.

Worth it? For anyone serious about cloud work, yes, clearly. Just go in with the right expectation: this is a cert that confirms experience rather than substitutes for it. Earn it after you've put your hands on AWS, not before, and it does exactly what you want a cert to do.

item.title: Attackers Are Exploiting a Netlogon Bug That Owns Domain Controllers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-41089, a 9.8-rated unauthenticated Netlogon flaw Microsoft patched in May, is now under active exploitation against domain controllers, and Belgium's cyber agency is sounding louder alarms than Redmond.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft patched it in May. Attackers are using it now. CVE-2026-41089 is a critical hole in the Windows Netlogon service, and the gap between the fix and the exploitation is exactly where unpatched domain controllers live.

The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in how Netlogon handles inbound RPC requests. A crafted packet with a malformed length field writes past the buffer and overwrites the return address on the stack. Because the Netlogon RPC interface is exposed on every domain controller by design, no authentication is needed to reach the vulnerable code. It carries a 9.8 CVSS score and affects Windows Server from 2012 through 2025.

Successful exploitation runs code inside the LSASS process on a domain controller. In practical terms, that's the whole Active Directory forest. Whoever lands this owns the directory that authenticates everything else.

What makes this one notable is who's doing the warning. Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity confirmed active exploitation on June 1 and told organizations to treat it as an emergency, roughly three weeks after Microsoft's May Patch Tuesday shipped the fix. The CCB's messaging has been blunter and more urgent than Microsoft's own, and there's been visible friction between the two over how the bug was communicated. When a national CSIRT is shouting louder than the vendor, that tells you how seriously to take it.

If your domain controllers aren't on the May 2026 cumulative update, that's the job for today. Netlogon RPC can't simply be firewalled off internally without breaking authentication, so patching is the real fix, not network controls. Confirm every DC is current, and review logs for unusual Netlogon RPC traffic and LSASS crashes that could mark a failed exploit attempt.

item.title: Network+ in 2026: Is It Worth It and How Hard Is the N10-009?
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Network+ sits in an awkward spot between A+ and CCNA, so the real question is whether the N10-009 earns a place in your path or whether you should jump to Cisco instead.
item.content:encoded:
Network+ has an identity problem, and pretending otherwise does no one any favors. It's vendor-neutral networking knowledge that nobody disputes is useful, sitting directly underneath Cisco's CCNA, which carries more weight with employers and costs about the same. So the honest framing for 2026 isn't "is Network+ good" (it is) but "is Network+ the right next step for you, or are you about to pay for a cert you'll outgrow in a year?"

Here are the facts on the current exam. The code is N10-009, and it replaced N10-008 when that retired in December 2024. It runs up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, mixing multiple choice with performance-based questions, and you need 720 out of 900 to pass. The retail price is $369 in the US. CompTIA recommends A+ first plus around nine to twelve months of hands-on networking experience, though plenty of people sit it earlier than that.

The exam splits into five domains: Networking Fundamentals (23%), Network Implementations (20%), Network Operations (19%), Network Security (14%), and Network Troubleshooting (24%). Note where the weight sits. Troubleshooting and fundamentals together are nearly half the exam, and that tells you what CompTIA is actually testing: not whether you can recite the OSI model, but whether you can reason through why a host can't reach a server.

How hard is it? Harder than A+, easier than CCNA. The conceptual load is real this time. Subnetting alone defeats more candidates than anything else on the exam, and you cannot fake your way through it. If binary math and CIDR notation make your eyes glaze, that's the wall you have to climb before you sit this. The good news is that subnetting is a learnable mechanical skill, not a talent, and a week of deliberate practice gets most people from lost to fluent.

Where Network+ pays off is the role it points at. The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the 2024 median for network and computer systems administrators around $97,000, well above the help desk tier A+ targets. Network+ is the credential that signals you're ready to step from support into administration. It's also DoD-approved for certain baseline roles, which matters if you're aiming at government or contractor work.

The study reality mirrors the exam's troubleshooting bias. Reading about VLANs and routing teaches you the words; configuring them teaches you the cert. The candidates who pass cleanly are the ones who spend real time in a lab simulating the networks they're being tested on, then drill a question bank to surface the subnetting and port-number gaps they didn't know they had. Theory-only studiers consistently underestimate the performance-based questions and pay for it on test day.

So: worth it, with a caveat. If you want vendor-neutral fundamentals or you need the DoD approval, Network+ is a clean, defensible choice. If your goal is squarely network engineering and you're comfortable committing, the CCNA covers similar ground with more market pull for the same money, and you can skip a step. Network+ is the safer, broader bet. CCNA is the more ambitious one. Neither is wrong; just be honest with yourself about which you're making.

item.title: A Perfect-10 Ivanti Sentry Bug Is Already Backdooring Gateways
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-10520, an unauthenticated command-injection flaw in Ivanti Sentry rated a maximum 10.0, is under active exploitation, and CISA gave federal agencies until June 14 to patch.
item.content:encoded:
A CVSS score of 10.0 is rare. Ivanti Sentry just earned one, and attackers were on it within a day.

Ivanti's June 9 advisory covers two bugs. CVE-2026-10520 is an OS command injection flaw that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker run code as root, and it sits at the maximum 10.0 severity. The second, CVE-2026-10523, is an authentication bypass at 9.9 that lets an attacker create their own admin accounts. Either one alone is bad. Chained, they hand over the box.

Sentry is the gateway that brokers access between mobile devices and an organization's internal mail and app servers, so it's exposed on purpose and it sits in a trusted spot on the network. That's the worst combination for a pre-auth root flaw. Affected versions are 10.5.1, 10.6.1, 10.7.0 and earlier; the fixes are in 10.5.2, 10.6.2, and 10.7.1.

This isn't theoretical. After watchTowr published a proof-of-concept, the Shadowserver Foundation started seeing exploitation attempts and confirmed backdoored gateways within 24 hours. CISA added CVE-2026-10520 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal civilian agencies just three days to patch, with a deadline of June 14.

Three days is CISA's way of saying this is on fire. Patch to the fixed releases now. If your Sentry was internet-facing and unpatched at any point this week, don't just patch and move on. Assume compromise, look for new admin accounts and unexpected processes running as root, and rotate any credentials that gateway could reach.

item.title: Is CompTIA A+ Worth It in 2026? An Honest Look at the 220-1201 and 1202
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A+ is two exams, real money, and a slow on-ramp into IT, so here's who it actually pays off for and who should skip straight past it.
item.content:encoded:
A+ is the cert people argue about most, and the argument is usually framed wrong. The question isn't whether A+ is respected (it's fine) or whether it's hard (it isn't, really). The question is whether you're the person it's built for. If you've never held an IT job and need something on your resume that says you can fix a laptop and not break the network, A+ does that job better than anything else. If you already work a help desk, it's mostly a box to check for HR.

The current version is two exams, not one. Core 1 (220-1201) and Core 2 (220-1202) both launched in March 2025 and replaced the older 1101/1102 pair, which CompTIA retired in September 2025. You need to pass both to earn the cert. Each exam runs up to 90 questions in 90 minutes. Core 1 wants 675 out of 900 to pass; Core 2 wants 700. Core 1 covers hardware, networking basics, mobile devices, and virtualization and cloud concepts. Core 2 is the software half: operating systems, security fundamentals, troubleshooting, and operational procedures.

Now the part nobody likes. At CompTIA's retail pricing each exam runs around $250 in the US, so you're looking at roughly $500 to sit both, before any study materials. That's the real sticker shock of A+, and it's worth saying plainly: this is the most expensive entry-level cert relative to the salary it points you toward.

Because where A+ lands you is the entry of the entry level. The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the 2024 median wage for computer user support specialists around $60,000 and computer network support specialists around $73,000. A+ is the credential that gets you in the door for the first of those, the help desk and desktop support roles where you'll spend a year or two before moving up. Treat it as a starting line, not a destination.

How hard is it? The content is broad rather than deep. There's a lot of it (printers, RAM types, Windows recovery, common malware, cable standards) but very little of it is conceptually difficult. The thing that trips people up is breadth plus the performance-based questions, where you have to actually do something in a simulated environment rather than pick an answer. People who only memorize acronyms get wrecked by those. People who've physically opened a machine and clicked around an OS sail through them.

That's the honest study advice for A+: stop reading and start touching things. Build a cheap PC or tear down an old one. Run a Windows install in a VM, break it, fix it. The candidates who pass comfortably are the ones who pair a video course with real hands-on reps and a question bank to find their weak spots before exam day, not the ones who read a 1,200-page book cover to cover. The terminology sticks far better once you've watched it happen in front of you.

So is it worth it in 2026? If you're switching careers into IT with nothing else to show, yes, and pairing it with Network+ or Security+ within the year is the move that actually changes your pay. If you already have a year of help desk under your belt, your time and money are better spent skipping ahead. A+ proves you can start. It was never meant to prove more than that.

item.title: ShinyHunters Hit 100+ Orgs Through an Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Oracle's out-of-band alert for CVE-2026-35273, a 9.8-rated unauthenticated RCE in PeopleSoft PeopleTools, lands after ShinyHunters had already used it to breach more than 100 organizations, most of them universities.
item.content:encoded:
More than a hundred organizations got breached before the vendor said a word. That's the shape of the Oracle PeopleSoft attack that came to light this week.

On June 10 Oracle put out an out-of-band Security Alert for CVE-2026-35273, a flaw in PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62. It's rated 9.8 on the CVSS scale: remote code execution, no authentication, no user interaction. An attacker who can reach the server over HTTP can run code on it. Because the attacks started before the alert went out, this was a true zero-day.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant tied the campaign to UNC6240, the crew that operates under the ShinyHunters name. They tracked the activity between May 27 and June 9, and the stolen data started showing up on the group's leak site on June 9. By the attackers' own count the campaign hit more than 100 organizations. Sixty-eight percent of the victims were in higher education, most of them in the United States.

The tradecraft is worth a look. The attackers stood up MeshCentral remote-management servers dressed up to look like legitimate cloud endpoints, registered a lookalike domain, and pushed a custom script to spread across networks and deface systems. This wasn't a smash-and-grab. It was a staged extortion operation that treated PeopleSoft as the front door to HR and student records.

There's a catch buried in Oracle's response. The alert points customers to a patch document, but that document sits behind a support login, so it isn't obvious to outsiders whether a full fix is even shipping yet. Oracle's headline guidance is mitigation: disable the Environment Management Hub service, or remove the PSEMHUB application entirely on single-server setups. Telling customers to rip out a component is not the same as handing them a patch.

If you run PeopleSoft, treat any internet-facing instance as suspect. Apply Oracle's mitigations now, hunt for unfamiliar MeshCentral agents and outbound connections to odd domains, and assume the EMHub component is the path attackers will try first. Education IT teams especially should check today, because that's where the attackers spent most of their time.

item.title: CompTIA CySA+ V4 Lands June 23: Sit the Old Exam or Wait?
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CompTIA's analyst cert gets a refresh on June 23 with new AI governance, cloud, and threat-hunting content, and if you're mid-prep you have a real decision to make.
item.content:encoded:
If you're studying for CySA+ right now, you've got a decision to make: sit the current exam before it ages out, or wait for the new one.

CompTIA launches CySA+ V4, exam code CS0-004, on June 23. The current version, CS0-003, stays available for a while after that. CompTIA usually runs about six months of overlap before retiring an old exam, though it hasn't put a firm retirement date on CS0-003 yet. Both versions carry the same name and certify the same thing; only the objectives differ.

V4 keeps the four-domain structure but reweights and modernizes it. The domains are Security Operations (34%), Vulnerability Management (26%), Incident Response and Management (24%), and Reporting and Communication (16%). The new material is where the cert catches up to the actual job: more cloud, a real emphasis on threat hunting, expanded identity and access management, and a fresh block on AI use cases, the risks they bring, and governance. Format is up to 85 questions in 165 minutes, with a passing score of 750 on a 100-to-900 scale.

Here's the practical call. If you're within a few weeks of testing and your material is built around CS0-003, finish what you started and sit the current exam. There's no penalty for holding a cert earned on the older objectives; it's the same credential on your resume. If you're earlier in your prep, or you work somewhere cloud-heavy or AI-adjacent, the V4 objectives map better to what you'll actually be doing, and that's worth waiting a few weeks for.

CySA+ is CompTIA's analyst cert, a step past Security+ and aimed at people doing detection, triage, and response rather than general security awareness. The V4 additions push it toward the SOC reality of 2026: cloud telemetry, hunting instead of waiting on alerts, and working out what to do when half your tooling suddenly has an AI feature bolted on. If that's the chair you sit in, or want to, the refresh is aimed at you.

One thing not to overthink, but to plan around: test-prep churn. New exam versions always arrive before the third-party practice questions and courses fully catch up. If you go for CS0-004 in its first month, lean on CompTIA's own objectives document over a hastily updated cram deck, and expect the AI and cloud sections to be the thinnest part of any third-party prep until the market fills them in.

item.title: OpenAI Models Are Coming to Oracle Cloud's Prepaid Credits
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Oracle Cloud customers will soon be able to spend their existing Universal Credits on OpenAI's models and Codex, turning a procurement headache into a budgeting line item.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI wants to sell its models to companies that never signed up for OpenAI. Its new deal with Oracle is how.

Under the partnership, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure customers will be able to spend their existing Oracle Universal Credits, the prepaid cloud commitments many enterprises already buy in bulk, on OpenAI's frontier models and its Codex coding agent. The models will be offered through the OCI Marketplace, and OpenAI says access arrives in the coming weeks.

There's no new model here and no new capability. What's new is the procurement path. For a large company, the friction in adopting OpenAI usually isn't technical; it's the legal and purchasing overhead of onboarding another vendor. Letting teams draw down a cloud commitment they already signed off on removes a step that quietly kills plenty of pilots before they start.

The two companies are already deep in business together. Oracle is one of the main compute providers behind OpenAI's data-center buildout, the Stargate effort, so wiring OpenAI's models into Oracle's marketplace is the customer-facing other half of an infrastructure deal that was mostly about who rents whom servers. This turns that plumbing into a sales channel.

It also tightens the knot. Every credit an Oracle customer spends on GPT through OCI is a credit they don't spend on a competing model, and it deepens the dependency between one cloud and one model vendor. Convenient for buyers today, and worth remembering the next time someone argues the AI market is still wide open.

For engineers the practical read is simple. If your shop runs on Oracle Cloud, getting GPT-class models and Codex into a project is about to be a budgeting question instead of a procurement project. That's a smaller change than a new model, and for a lot of teams it will matter more.

item.title: CISA: Patch the Actively Exploited SolarWinds Serv-U Flaw by June 19
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-28318 lets an unauthenticated attacker crash SolarWinds Serv-U with a single crafted POST request, and CISA has set a June 19 deadline to fix it.
item.content:encoded:
SolarWinds is back on CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities list, this time for a flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker knock its Serv-U file-transfer server offline with a single crafted request.

CVE-2026-28318 is an uncontrolled resource consumption bug. A remote attacker with no credentials can trigger it by sending an HTTP POST request carrying a Content-Encoding: deflate header, which forces Serv-U to chew through resources until the service crashes. Every version up to and including 15.5.4 is affected. SolarWinds fixed it in Serv-U 15.5.4 Hotfix 1.

It's a denial-of-service bug, not remote code execution, so nobody is stealing files through this one directly. But Serv-U is managed file-transfer software, the kind of appliance that sits at the edge of a network moving sensitive data between partners. Knocking it down on demand is disruptive on its own, and DoS against file-transfer gear has a habit of being either a precursor or a distraction.

CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 5 and gave federal civilian agencies until June 19 to patch. That window is nearly shut. A KEV listing isn't theoretical: CISA only adds bugs it has evidence are being used in real attacks.

Serv-U has been here before. The same product showed up in CISA's catalog for a path-traversal flaw in 2024 and a remote-code-execution bug in 2021 that was tied to state-linked activity. For software whose entire job is to sit exposed and move files, that's a track record worth weighing when you decide how fast to act.

If you run Serv-U, get to 15.5.4 Hotfix 1. If you can't patch right away, SolarWinds and CISA point to the same stopgaps: put the service behind a WAF or firewall so only known addresses can reach it, and block POST requests that include a content-encoding header. Neither is a real substitute for the fix.

item.title: Researcher Drops 'RoguePlanet' Defender Zero-Day Hours After Patch Tuesday
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A working exploit called RoguePlanet escalates a local user to SYSTEM on fully patched Windows 10 and 11 through a Microsoft Defender race condition, and there's no fix yet.
item.content:encoded:
Hours after Microsoft shipped its June Patch Tuesday this week, a researcher published a working exploit for a Defender bug Microsoft hasn't patched at all.

The exploit, called RoguePlanet, abuses a race condition in Microsoft Defender's quarantine pipeline to escalate a local user to SYSTEM, the highest privilege level on Windows. The researcher, who goes by Nightmare Eclipse, says it works on fully patched Windows 10 and Windows 11. There's no CVE assigned and no fix available.

This is local privilege escalation, not remote code execution, so an attacker needs a foothold on the machine first. But that's exactly the second stage of most intrusions: phish a user, land as a low-privilege account, then climb. A reliable SYSTEM escalation that survives a fully updated Defender install is the kind of primitive ransomware crews and access brokers pay real money for.

RoguePlanet isn't this researcher's first drop. Microsoft has already patched a run of Defender bugs Nightmare Eclipse disclosed: RedSun (CVE-2026-41091, fixed out-of-band on May 21 and later added to CISA's known-exploited list), UnDefend (CVE-2026-45498), and BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825), all reported as exploited in the wild before patches landed.

The researcher has been blunt about the motive. Nightmare Eclipse frames the public drops as a response to how Microsoft handled earlier reports, citing a disclosure process that let bugs sit and a working relationship that went bad. Whatever the rights and wrongs, the practical result is that defenders are learning about a SYSTEM-level Defender flaw from exploit code instead of an advisory.

Microsoft hadn't issued guidance as of this writing. Until it does, the usual containment holds: tighten local admin rights, watch for odd Defender child processes spawning with SYSTEM privileges, and treat any machine an attacker can already touch as a machine they can own. If exploitation picks up, expect an out-of-band patch rather than a wait for July.

item.title: SpaceX Prices the Largest IPO Ever, Debuts on Nasdaq Tomorrow
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SpaceX set its IPO at $135 a share, a $1.77 trillion valuation that raises about $75 billion and makes it the seventh-biggest US company before it has even started trading.
item.content:encoded:
Seventy-five billion dollars. That's what SpaceX is set to raise when shares start trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow under the ticker SPCX, in what will be the largest initial public offering ever recorded.

SpaceX priced the offering at $135 a share and is selling about 555.6 million shares. At that price the company is valued at roughly $1.77 trillion, more than triple the size of Alibaba's 2014 listing, the previous record for a US debut. SpaceX would immediately rank as the seventh-largest US company by market cap, sitting above Tesla, Musk's other big holding, which is worth around $1.6 trillion.

The thing going public isn't just rockets. Musk merged SpaceX with his AI company xAI in February in a deal that valued the combined business at $1.25 trillion, so the shares cover three operations at once: the launch business, the Starlink satellite-internet network, and the xAI unit behind the Grok models. Anyone buying SPCX is buying all of it in a single ticket.

Musk will hold over 82% of the voting power after the offering. Public shareholders get the upside and almost no say in how the company is run. That arrangement has become standard for founder-led tech listings, but the gap here is wide even by that bar.

Starlink is the part carrying the valuation. Recurring subscription revenue across millions of terminals is the closest thing SpaceX has to a predictable cash machine, and it's what lets bankers justify a number that would be hard to defend for a launch company alone. The rocket side is still capital-hungry, and Starship's reusable economics look promising but aren't yet proven at the flight cadence the model assumes.

For index funds, the debut creates an immediate headache. A company this size joining public markets means trillions in passively managed money will have to buy SPCX whether the managers love the price or not. Plenty of retail investors will own a slice of SpaceX by tomorrow afternoon without ever choosing to.

item.title: CCNA v2.0 Lands February 2027: Troubleshooting Is Back and AI Is In
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Cisco's refreshed 200-301 v2.0 exam puts the troubleshoot verb on more than a quarter of its topics, adds an AI section, and trims six domains down to five.
item.content:encoded:
Cisco has set the date: CCNA 200-301 version 2.0 goes live on February 3, 2027. The current v1.1 exam stays valid right up until the cutover, so every candidate studying today has a decision to make.

The headline change is troubleshooting. In the v2.0 blueprint, 28% of exam topics use the verb 'troubleshoot,' and that's a bigger deal than it sounds. Troubleshooting essentially vanished from the CCNA in the 2020 revision and stayed gone through v1.1. For six years you could pass by knowing how things are configured. Starting next February, Cisco wants to know whether you can figure out why they're broken.

There's also a new AI section covering prompt construction and foundational AI security concepts. Before you roll your eyes, it's a small slice of the blueprint, and it reflects what's actually showing up in network operations tooling. The domain structure consolidates from six domains to five, the exam stays 120 minutes, and a pass still earns the same CCNA certification.

So: rush v1.1 or wait for v2.0? If you're months into prep, finish on v1.1 before February 2027. Your study materials match the live exam, the certification you earn is identical, and nobody's resume distinguishes which blueprint version they passed. If you're starting from zero in late 2026, it gets closer; you may be better served studying toward v2.0 since the skills it tests are the ones interviews actually probe.

Either way, the troubleshooting shift changes how you should study more than what you should study. You can't flashcard your way through 'troubleshoot OSPF adjacency.' You need broken configs and time on a CLI, whether that's a simulator, rented rack time, or used gear off eBay. Candidates who built their prep on reading will feel this revision. Candidates who built it on labs won't notice much difference, which is presumably Cisco's point.

item.title: Apple's New Siri Runs on Google's Model, and Apple Said So Out Loud
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: At WWDC 2026 Apple rebranded its assistant as Siri AI, confirmed it runs a custom Gemini model in Apple's data centers, and opened iOS 27 to rival chatbots.
item.content:encoded:
The most consequential thing Apple said at WWDC on June 8 was an admission: the long-promised Siri overhaul is finally here, it's called Siri AI, and the intelligence underneath is a custom version of Google's Gemini.

The arrangement, reportedly worth about a billion dollars a year to Google, runs Gemini-based models inside Apple's own data centers behind Private Cloud Compute, with on-device processing handling what it can. Apple gets a frontier model without having trained one; Google gets paid and gets its model onto the most valuable install base in consumer tech. Both companies know exactly what this echoes, because they've run the same play with search for fifteen years.

The assistant itself finally does what was promised in 2024: cross-app actions, on-screen awareness, and personal context, plus a dedicated Siri app that keeps conversation history and works on iPad and Mac. Demos looked fluid, though WWDC demos always do. The original Apple Intelligence Siri was announced two years ago and partially shipped late; skepticism until this is on real devices is earned.

The quieter announcement may matter more. In iOS 27, Apple is opening Siri's handoff mechanism beyond ChatGPT so users can route requests to other chatbots, with Claude and Gemini named in early reporting. Apple is positioning itself as the aggregation point for AI assistants rather than a competitor to any of them, which is a strong position to retreat to when you've conceded the model race.

The rest of the keynote was a platform tour: iOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, and the usual cadence across watchOS, tvOS, and visionOS, with Liquid Glass refinements and AI woven through the system apps rather than headlined.

Strip the privacy framing and the shape of the deal is plain: Apple is now a distribution channel for someone else's intelligence, and it's betting the customer relationship is worth more than the model. With search, that bet paid roughly twenty billion dollars a year. The difference is that nobody asked their search engine to know everything about them.

item.title: OpenAI Files for Its IPO. The Math Underneath Is the Real Story
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI confirmed a confidential S-1 targeting a September debut at $730 to $850 billion, while reportedly losing more than a dollar for every dollar it earns.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI confirmed on June 8 that it has confidentially filed for a US IPO, targeting a debut as soon as September at a valuation between $730 and $850 billion. The S-1 reportedly went to the SEC around May 22; the public only heard about it once the company chose to say so.

Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and JPMorgan are leading the offering, and some analysts are already talking past the filing range toward a trillion-dollar print. That would make it the largest tech IPO ever by a wide margin.

Hold that number next to this one: OpenAI was generating about $2 billion in monthly revenue as of March, but an analysis of its recent financials found it lost roughly $1.22 for every dollar it earned in the quarter. The revenue curve is extraordinary. So is the burn. An IPO at this moment reads less like a victory lap and more like the logical next step for a company whose appetite for compute has outgrown what private markets can comfortably feed it.

The timing isn't happening in a vacuum. Anthropic filed for its own IPO on June 1 at a reported $965 billion valuation, SpaceX is in the pipeline, and Bloomberg now tallies the AI IPO queue at $3.6 trillion in combined paper value. Two frontier labs going public in the same half-year means public markets, not private mega-rounds, are about to set the price of the AI boom for the first time.

One more wrinkle: the confirmation landed hours after Apple's WWDC keynote, where the new Siri was revealed to run on Google's Gemini. OpenAI's ChatGPT handoff deal made it the default AI brand on the iPhone; that exclusivity is now visibly eroding right as the company asks the public to price its consumer moat.

The S-1 will eventually become public, and with it the first audited look at OpenAI's actual economics: real margins, real compute obligations, real revenue concentration. Every claim about AI economics to date has been sourced from leaks and investor decks. The prospectus is where the story has to survive an auditor.

item.title: Critical Veeam Flaw Lets Any Domain User Run Code on Your Backup Server
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-44963 (CVSS 9.4) gives any low-privilege domain account remote code execution on domain-joined Veeam Backup & Replication v12 servers; the fix shipped June 9.
item.content:encoded:
Any domain account, including the intern's, can now potentially execute code on the server that holds your backups. That's the short version of CVE-2026-44963, a critical flaw in Veeam Backup & Replication that scored 9.4 on CVSS v4.

The vulnerability affects version 12.3.2.4465 and every earlier v12 build. Veeam shipped the fix in 12.3.2.4854 on June 9, documented in KB4696. Version 13 isn't affected thanks to architectural changes, which is a quiet argument for the upgrade if you've been putting it off. The bug was found and reported by Sina Kheirkhah of watchTowr.

There's one important catch: only domain-joined backup servers are exposed. Veeam's own hardening guidance has said for years that backup infrastructure should live outside Active Directory, in a workgroup, precisely so a compromised domain doesn't take the backups down with it. Plenty of shops domain-join anyway because it makes management easier. This CVE is the bill for that convenience.

Why this one deserves your attention over the average critical: ransomware crews go after backup infrastructure first, before they encrypt anything, because organizations with intact backups don't pay. A reliable path from any low-privilege domain account to code execution on the Veeam server is exactly the primitive those playbooks are built around. No exploitation has been reported yet, but patch-diffing starts the moment a fix ships, and Veeam flaws have historically gone from patch to active exploitation within weeks.

Patch to 12.3.2.4854 now, and if your backup server is domain-joined, treat this as the prompt to fix that too. The patch closes this CVE. Pulling the server out of the domain closes the next one.

item.title: June Patch Tuesday: 200 Fixes, Six Zero-Days, and a Bug Bounty Protest
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft's June update patches an actively exploited Exchange spoofing flaw plus five publicly disclosed zero-days, several of them dropped by a group protesting how Redmond runs its bounty program.
item.content:encoded:
Two hundred vulnerabilities, 33 of them critical, six zero-days, and one of those already being used in attacks. Microsoft's June Patch Tuesday is one of the largest of the year, and the story behind several of the zero-days is messier than the usual coordinated-disclosure routine.

Patch the Exchange flaw first. CVE-2026-42897, a spoofing vulnerability in Exchange Server, is the only bug in the batch confirmed to be actively exploited. If you still run on-prem Exchange, you already know the drill: it remains one of the most reliably attacked products in enterprise IT, and a spoofing primitive there tends to be the first link in a phishing or mailbox-takeover chain.

Five more zero-days were publicly disclosed before patches existed, and most of them trace to a group calling itself Nightmare Eclipse, which dropped GreenPlasma (CVE-2026-45586, a Windows CTFMON privilege escalation), the YellowKey BitLocker bypass (CVE-2026-45585), and Mini-Plasma in protest of how Microsoft handles its bug bounty and disclosure programs. Whatever you think of the tactic, it worked as pressure: all of them got fixed this cycle.

The remaining disclosures came through more conventional channels. Researchers at Calif.io documented an HTTP/2 Bomb denial-of-service flaw in HTTP.sys (CVE-2026-49160), and Jonas Lykkegaard published a second BitLocker bypass dubbed bitskrieg (CVE-2026-50507). Two separate BitLocker bypasses in one month is worth pausing on if your threat model includes lost or stolen laptops, since both undermine the assumption that disk encryption protects a powered-off machine.

The oddest entry is CVE-2020-17103, a Windows Cloud Files Mini Filter Driver flaw that Google Project Zero's James Forshaw originally reported in September 2020. It carries a 2020 CVE number and is only now getting a patch. Microsoft hasn't explained the five-and-a-half-year gap.

For prioritization: Exchange first, then the BitLocker bypasses on any fleet with mobile hardware, then work through the criticals. Twenty-eight of the 33 critical-rated bugs are remote code execution, and the elevation-of-privilege pile (65 bugs this month) is what attackers chain after initial access. The protest angle makes good copy, but the patching order is the part that matters by Friday.

item.title: A Worm Built for AI Coding Tools Took Down 73 Microsoft GitHub Repos
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Miasma worm planted credential-stealing payloads that fire when a repo is opened in Claude Code, Cursor, or VS Code, forcing GitHub to disable 73 official Microsoft repositories.
item.content:encoded:
It took GitHub 105 seconds to pull 73 of Microsoft's own repositories offline. The infection that forced the takedown had been spreading for more than two weeks before anyone hit the kill switch.

On June 5, GitHub disabled repositories across four official Microsoft organizations: Azure, Azure-Samples, MicrosoftDocs, and Microsoft itself. The trigger was a malicious commit pushed to Azure/durabletask through a previously compromised contributor account. The commit planted configuration files that execute a credential-harvesting payload the moment a developer opens the repository in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code. The worm doesn't attack the code you ship. It attacks the tools you write it with.

The malware, dubbed Miasma, is assessed to be a variant of the Mini Shai-Hulud worm that the TeamPCP group publicly released in mid-May. The chain traces back to May 19, when the durabletask package on PyPI (Microsoft's Azure Durable Task SDK) was compromised. Three malicious versions went live within 35 minutes, published using GitHub Actions secrets the attackers had already stolen.

This is the uncomfortable part: agentic coding tools are designed to read and act on repository configuration automatically. Hooks, instruction files, and tool manifests get parsed and executed as a feature. The old supply chain model assumed a human would at least glance at the code before running it. The new one assumes your AI assistant will open whatever it's pointed at, and Miasma was written by someone who understood that perfectly.

Microsoft has restored some of the repositories while keeping others offline as the investigation continues, and this is reportedly the second time Miasma has hit the company's GitHub presence. Neither Microsoft nor GitHub has published a full accounting of which repos carried the payload and for how long, which makes it hard for downstream teams to know whether they were exposed.

If you or your tooling touched Microsoft's GitHub orgs or the durabletask package since mid-May, rotate credentials now, especially GitHub tokens and cloud keys that live in your environment. Then look at the agent-facing config of every repo you clone before you let an AI tool loose in it. That file your assistant helpfully reads on startup is now an execution vector.

item.title: The Cisco SD-WAN Bug from Yesterday is a Textbook Security+ PBQ
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Walking through CVE-2026-20122 as a SY0-701 objective 2.3 performance-based question. What the attack actually abuses, and why most candidates pick the wrong control.
item.content:encoded:
We covered the Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager CVEs yesterday. Emergency Directive 26-03, three exploits under active use, federal patch deadline today. CVE-2026-20122, the file-overwrite flaw that escalates a caller to vmanage user, is also a clean Security+ performance-based question. Walking through it teaches the exam logic better than a generic textbook example of missing authorization.

Here is the bug in one paragraph. A privileged API endpoint accepts a file upload from an authenticated caller. The endpoint does not check whether the caller is authorized to call it. The file gets written to a location that executes with vmanage privileges, so a lower-privilege account walks away with vmanage. The upload itself is not the security hole. The authorization check that was never wired up is.

The mapping to SY0-701 objective 2.3 ("Explain various types of vulnerabilities") is where candidates slip. The objective lists a lot of bug shapes — improper input handling, unprotected APIs, privilege escalation, misconfiguration. A PBQ typically gives you the symptom and asks for two things: classify the vuln, pick the compensating control. Most candidates see "file upload" and pick input validation. Wrong answer. The OWASP API Security Top 10 pegs this as API5:2023, Broken Function Level Authorization. On the exam, the keyword cluster is "improper access control" and "privilege escalation," and the control is role-based access control on the API surface, not input sanitization.

The reason input-validation is the wrong answer is worth sitting with. If you harden the parser and reject malformed uploads, the authenticated low-privilege attacker still calls the API, still uploads the file, still escalates. You stopped a different attack. This one goes through clean input.

If you can describe CVE-2026-20122 in two sentences — "privileged API trusted an unauthorized caller; file upload was the side effect, not the root cause" — you can answer any PBQ that tests the same shape. The shape shows up across Sec+, CySA+ (objective 1.4 vulnerability analysis), and PenTest+ (objective 3.6 API testing). Read the CVE advisory itself, not the CVSS line. The CVSS is a score; the advisory is the story.

Tomorrow's QoD will walk a related one. Try it before reading the explanation.

item.title: A Four-Month-Old AI Lab with 20 Employees Just Raised Half a Billion Dollars
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Recursive Superintelligence closed a $500M round at a $4B pre-money valuation, led by GV with Nvidia participating. It has been incorporated since December.
item.content:encoded:
Recursive Superintelligence, an AI startup that did not exist at the end of last year, has raised at least $500 million at a $4 billion pre-money valuation. GV led the round. Nvidia joined. Per reporting from the Financial Times, the company has been operating for roughly four months and has under two dozen employees.

The headcount matters. A lab raising at this scale with twenty people is a bet on who the twenty people are, not what the product is. That is the shape of seed-stage frontier-AI fundraising now: partnerships write nine-figure checks based on pedigree and a deck, because the alternative is being shut out once capability compounds.

The company's stated thesis is recursive self-improvement, meaning models that improve their own training process. That phrase has been floating around AI labs for a decade, but it takes on weight when Nvidia decides to put its balance sheet behind a specific team pursuing it. Nvidia is the one vendor in the industry with real signal on who is actually building capable systems, because everyone buys chips from them.

There is no public product, no demos, no paper. Whatever Recursive Superintelligence is building will stay behind closed doors until either a research result or a capability demonstration justifies the valuation. In the meantime, the round itself is the story.

Two things to watch. First, the employee count in six months. If it stays small, the thesis is a compute-and-autonomy play where a handful of researchers drive everything.
