If it triples, the real work is operational and this was a talent-acquisition round dressed up as a seed. Second, whether GV's involvement draws in Google's own infrastructure. That would be the quiet signal that someone at Google thinks this team is worth a hedge outside DeepMind.

item.title: OpenAI Built a Less-Restricted AI Model for Security Teams. Anthropic Went the Other Direction.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI's GPT-5.4-Cyber rolled out April 14 to thousands of verified defenders. Anthropic's Mythos went to about 40 organizations. Two labs looked at the same capability tier and drew opposite conclusions.
item.content:encoded:
Six days apart. On April 8, Anthropic confirmed its most capable model, Claude Mythos, would not be publicly released, with access restricted to roughly 40 partners under Project Glasswing. On April 14, OpenAI announced GPT-5.4-Cyber, a version of its frontier model with relaxed restrictions for legitimate security work, and rolled it out to thousands of verified defenders through a program called Trusted Access for Cyber.

Read those two decisions together and the disagreement is explicit. Anthropic concluded that a model capable of autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploit chaining was too dangerous to distribute widely, regardless of the caller's stated purpose. OpenAI concluded that the right answer to dangerous capability is not scarcity, but verification — make sure the caller is who they say they are, and then let the capability serve defense at scale.

Both positions have force. Anthropic's is the more conservative call, and the one that holds up if something goes wrong downstream: if a restricted-tier model gets used to automate mass-scale intrusion, the lab that shipped it to thousands of customers is the one at the hearing. OpenAI's is the more operationally honest call: attackers don't wait for approval to use AI tooling, and the defensive side of the asymmetry has been outpaced for two years. Getting capable tools into the hands of defenders at a scale that matches the threat is worth the verification overhead.

The quiet part is that both companies appear to believe the underlying capability threshold has actually been crossed. Neither is shipping its best model into the public API with default safety training. Both have converged on gated-access programs tied to identity verification. The disagreement is about how wide the gate is, not whether there should be one.

For security teams, the immediate question is which program your organization qualifies for and which one actually improves your defensive posture. The OpenAI program is easier to get into and covers thousands of organizations. The Anthropic program is smaller, tighter, and reportedly pairs access with direct partnership support. A third interesting question: what happens when the next tier above both of these gets built. Neither company has committed to what they'll do at that point, and the answers they give in April 2027 are going to matter more than the ones they're giving now.

item.title: Anthropic Is Holding Back Its Most Capable Model. That's a First.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Claude Mythos won't ship publicly. Access is limited to select partners under Project Glasswing, citing cybersecurity risk. The frontier just developed an unshipped tier.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic confirmed on April 7 what a March 26 internal leak had already made plain: its most capable model, internally called Claude Mythos, will not be publicly released. Access is restricted to a small number of partners under a program the company is calling Project Glasswing, with cybersecurity risk cited as the reason.

This is new territory. Every frontier lab up to now — OpenAI, Google DeepMind, xAI, Meta, Anthropic itself — has shipped its most capable model to end users, with guardrails layered on top. The implicit deal was: capability is the product, and we'll moderate the dangerous edges at inference time. Project Glasswing breaks that pattern.

The cybersecurity specifics Anthropic pointed to are not hand-wavy. Mythos reportedly demonstrated strong performance on autonomous exploitation chains — finding vulnerabilities, writing working exploits against them, and chaining them through multi-step intrusions without human guidance at the individual steps. That's the capability class that has kept national-security researchers nervous for two years. It's apparently here.

The industry reaction will be interesting to watch. If Anthropic's competitors have models at or near this capability tier, they now face a harder decision about whether to ship theirs. If they ship and something bad happens downstream — mass-scale automated intrusion, for example — Anthropic's restraint becomes evidence at whatever hearing follows. If they don't ship, the commercial pressure of holding back a working model while Anthropic's partners extract value from theirs is significant.

One thing worth flagging: the only public information we have about Mythos's actual capabilities comes from Anthropic itself and the March leak. There's no independent red-team writeup, no external benchmark report. Trust-but-verify applies as much to a company restraining a model as one releasing it.

For teams building on the Claude API, this doesn't change anything today — the publicly available Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 lines continue to ship and evolve. But the existence of a deliberately unshipped tier above them is the story everyone in the space is going to be chewing on for months.

item.title: India Stood Up a Formal AI Governance Body. It Left Out the Sector Regulators.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The AI Governance and Economic Group, formed April 13, excludes RBI, SEBI, TRAI, and CCI — the regulators the country's own AI guidelines named as essential. The membership is ministers and IT officials only.
item.content:encoded:
India formed its central AI governance body, the AI Governance and Economic Group (AIGEG), on April 13. It is chaired by Union IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and will coordinate AI policy across ministries. The group's purpose, per the MeitY announcement, is to serve as the country's institutional mechanism for steering national AI strategy.

What is missing from the AIGEG roster is the story. The India AI Governance Guidelines, published by the same ministry earlier this year, explicitly recommended that sectoral regulators — the Reserve Bank of India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the Telecom Regulatory Authority, and the Competition Commission — retain domain-specific AI enforcement and participate in the central coordination mechanism. The AIGEG as constituted has none of them.

Instead, membership is limited to ministers and senior officials from a handful of ministries, with a separate Technology and Policy Expert Committee (TPEC) supplying advisory input. The TPEC is an advisory body. It does not wield enforcement authority or supervisory power. That leaves the AIGEG as a purely inter-ministerial coordination forum that formally has jurisdiction over AI policy cutting across financial services, telecom, and competition, without the regulators who actually run those domains inside the tent.

There are two ways to read this. The charitable reading: MeitY wanted a fast-moving body of political principals and will loop regulators in through the TPEC as needed. The less charitable reading: the sectoral regulators were excluded because a body that includes RBI and SEBI is a body where AI rules get shaped by people with statutory mandates, and MeitY wanted policy that moves on executive timelines rather than regulatory ones.

The practical consequence for anyone building AI products into regulated Indian sectors is a coordination problem. If the AIGEG issues a position on financial-services AI and RBI reaches a different conclusion through its own supervisory process, the question of which one binds a regulated entity is unsettled. Indian AI governance just became more centralized on paper and more fragmented in practice.

item.title: ISC2 Quietly Cut 31 Certifications from the CISSP Experience Waiver List
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Effective April 1, CEH, CISA, CRISC, OSCP, and most GIAC credentials no longer count toward the one-year CISSP experience waiver. The new list is about half the size of the old one.
item.content:encoded:
ISC2 cut its CISSP experience-waiver list from roughly 50 credentials to 25 on April 1. The move went live with minimal marketing, and most candidates didn't notice until they went to submit. If your planned path to CISSP assumed a specific cert would shave a year off the five-year experience requirement, check the list before you file.

The removed certifications include CEH, CISA, CRISC, OSCP, and most of the GIAC catalog. Only four GIAC creds survive: GICSP, GISF, GISP, and GSLC. That is a significant narrowing. OSCP and CRISC in particular were heavily used by candidates coming in from offensive security and audit backgrounds who now lose a year of waiver.

What stays on the list: CompTIA Security+, CySA+, CASP+, ISC2's own SSCP and CCSP, ISACA CISM, and ISC2's concentration credentials ISSAP, ISSEP, and ISSMP. The pattern is visible once you read it. ISC2 kept the credentials that sit below CISSP in vendor hierarchies and the management-tier credentials that don't compete with CISSP directly. It trimmed the credentials that arguably prove equal-or-greater depth on specific technical domains.

The reasoning ISC2 has offered privately amounts to: the waiver was being used to shortcut into CISSP by candidates who hadn't actually done five years of covered domain work. That's defensible in theory. In practice, a candidate with OSCP and two years at a red team shop arguably knows the security assessment domain better than most CISSPs do, and that person now waits an extra year to sit the exam.

If you were planning to file a waiver application, the date that matters is April 1, 2026. Applications submitted before that date are grandfathered under the old list. If you already hold one of the removed credentials and can document five years of domain work, you don't need the waiver at all. Everyone else is doing the math again.

item.title: NIST Is Giving Up on Fully Enriching Every CVE. Your Patch Management Probably Depends on That.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The National Vulnerability Database will now prioritize enrichment instead of covering everything. Teams that treated NVD as the authoritative source just got a new dependency problem.
item.content:encoded:
NIST announced this week that the National Vulnerability Database is changing how it handles CVEs — prioritizing enrichment for a subset of submissions rather than attempting full coverage. The stated driver: a 263% surge in CVE submissions between 2020 and 2025. The team simply can't keep up.

If you've built your vulnerability management program on NVD data — and most organizations have, because it's been the authoritative free source for CVSS scores, CPE mappings, and structured metadata — this affects you directly.

The practical consequence: some CVEs will appear in NVD with limited enrichment. No CPE match strings. No CVSS vector string. Maybe no severity at all. Your scanner or SBOM tool that joins against NVD to decide what's critical will miss things or return nulls. The gap is going to land hardest on mid-tier vendors and open-source libraries, where CNA submissions are often sparse to begin with.

There's a reasonable counter-argument to make here — NVD was never going to scale linearly with CVE volume, and fully enriching every low-quality submission was diluting the signal of the serious ones. Prioritization might produce better data on the CVEs that actually matter. We'll see.

What to do this week: audit where your vulnerability workflow treats NVD as a single source of truth. Cross-reference against CISA KEV, vendor advisories, and at least one commercial feed (Tenable, Qualys, Snyk, whoever you already pay) so you're not blind on any CVE that NVD deprioritizes. The days of a free, complete, structured CVE database are ending, and you need an answer for that before your next audit.

One quiet note: this also puts more pressure on CISA's KEV catalog as the thing federal agencies and serious private-sector programs actually trigger patching off of. KEV is curated, conservative, and only covers actively exploited bugs — which is exactly why it's been more operationally useful than NVD for years anyway.

item.title: Everest Is Claiming Citizens Bank and Frost Bank in a Wave of Financial Sector Hits
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Everest ransomware group posted both US banks to its leak site on April 20, alongside four other victims across aviation, automotive, and retail. The claimed haul includes 250,000 SSNs and 3.4 million banking records.
item.content:encoded:
The Everest ransomware group claimed two major US banks on its leak site on April 20: Frost Bank in San Antonio and Citizens Bank. Both listings went up the same day, as part of a broader batch that also names Tokoparts, Complete Aircraft Group, Umiles Group, and Nutrabio. Neither bank has confirmed the claim publicly as of this writing.

Everest says it exfiltrated more than 380 GB from the financial targets. The breakdown it posted includes 250,000-plus Social Security numbers and Tax Identification Numbers, 3.4 million banking records, unencrypted credit card details, and complete employee email archives. Treat every number in a ransomware group's own public claim as a high estimate until a victim confirms, but the categories here are plausible for what a bank would actually hold.

Everest's tradecraft has shifted over the last year toward initial access via infostealer logs rather than in-house intrusion capability. The group buys credentials harvested from infected employee endpoints, walks them into corporate VPNs and SaaS admin consoles, and moves laterally from there. That matters for financial-sector defenders because the entry point is not your perimeter or your EDR coverage. It is an employee's personal laptop, a contractor's reused password, or a home machine that happened to be logged into a work account when it got hit by a commodity stealer.

Frost Bank and Citizens Bank are different animals. Frost is a regional bank, heavily concentrated in Texas, with a traditionally conservative technology posture. Citizens is a top-15 US bank by deposits with a far larger attack surface and a consumer base that will care loudly if the 3.4 million records figure holds up.

The practical move for banking customers at either institution: enable transaction alerts, freeze credit at all three bureaus, and watch for targeted phishing that name-drops the bank to establish familiarity. Attackers know exactly which records they took and who they took them from. Expect the phishing to be specific.

item.title: CISA Added Eight CVEs to KEV Yesterday. Three Hit Cisco SD-WAN and the Federal Deadline Is Thursday.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-20122, CVE-2026-20128, and CVE-2026-20133 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager are all under active exploitation. Federal civilian agencies have until April 23 to patch or disconnect.
item.content:encoded:
CISA added eight vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on April 20. Three of them are in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager. All three are under active exploitation per CISA, and federal civilian agencies have until April 23 to patch or disconnect the affected systems under Emergency Directive 26-03.

The three Cisco CVEs. CVE-2026-20122 (CVSS 5.4) allows an attacker to abuse a privileged API to upload and overwrite arbitrary files and gain vmanage user privileges. CVE-2026-20128 (CVSS 7.5) is a recoverable password storage flaw that lets an authenticated local attacker obtain DCA user credentials. CVE-2026-20133 (CVSS 6.5) is an unauthorized-access flaw that leaks sensitive information to a remote attacker.

The CVSS scores look modest. The operational impact doesn't. SD-WAN Manager controls the orchestration plane for enterprise and federal branch connectivity. An attacker chaining a file-overwrite into credential disclosure into information leakage has a working path into tenant configuration, certificate material, and the underlying management layer for every managed appliance in a deployment. CISA's decision to pair the KEV additions with an emergency directive signals that the exploitation chain is being used against federal systems right now, not theoretically.

The rest of the April 20 KEV batch includes vulnerabilities in PaperCut NG/MF, JetBrains TeamCity, Kentico Xperience, Quest KACE Systems Management Appliance, and Synacor Zimbra Collaboration Suite. Each one is the kind of internet-exposed enterprise middleware that ransomware affiliates live on.

The April 23 deadline is two days away. If you run Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, the only question this week is whether your patch window closes before CISA's does. Inventory affected versions, apply Cisco's fixes, and rotate any credentials stored on the management nodes as if they are already burned. If patching isn't available by Thursday, disconnect the management plane from the internet until it is. The directive applies to federal agencies, but private-sector operators running the same appliance should treat the deadline as their own.

item.title: Attackers Found a 13-Year-Old RCE in Apache ActiveMQ's Management Interface
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-34197 abuses ActiveMQ's Jolokia JMX-HTTP bridge to execute arbitrary code — effectively without credentials on certain 6.x versions — and CISA wants federal agencies patched by April 30.
item.content:encoded:
The Jolokia management endpoint in Apache ActiveMQ has been shipping enabled by default for 13 years. CVE-2026-34197 is what happens when researchers finally pull on it.

The vulnerability is a code injection flaw in the Jolokia JMX-HTTP bridge that ActiveMQ exposes for monitoring and administration. An attacker who can reach that endpoint can call the BrokerService MBean and force the broker to fetch a remote Spring XML configuration file they control. The JVM then executes it. CVSS score is 8.8, technically requiring low-privilege credentials — but that bar has a structural hole in it.

On ActiveMQ versions 6.0.0 through 6.1.1, CVE-2024-32114 (a separate, widely undeployed patch) leaves the Jolokia API exposed with no authentication whatsoever. An organization that upgraded to the 6.x branch for its features but hasn't kept up with every subsequent patch is running what is functionally unauthenticated remote code execution. Default credentials (admin:admin) make it nearly as bad on many 5.x deployments where nobody has changed the defaults.

Horizon3.ai disclosed the vulnerability after researchers used AI-assisted code analysis to trace the Jolokia invocation path as a viable attacker-controlled sink. A 13-year-old critical flaw sitting in a default-enabled management API, not found by prior manual audits. It's a reasonable argument for running AI-augmented code review across legacy open-source projects with large exposed attack surfaces.

CISA added CVE-2026-34197 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal civilian agencies until April 30 to patch or disconnect affected systems. SAFE Security documented active exploitation against internet-exposed Jolokia endpoints, particularly deployments running default or no authentication.

Patch to ActiveMQ 5.19.4 or 6.2.3. If patching isn't immediate, block external access to port 8161 (the admin console) at your firewall. Run a query on your IP ranges for exposed ActiveMQ instances (Shodan and Censys both index these) and assume any unpatched, internet-reachable broker with default credentials has already been touched.

item.title: Four Critical CVEs in Cisco ISE and Webex, Three of Them at CVSS 9.9
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-20147 gives an attacker with read-only ISE admin credentials a path to root on your network access control infrastructure, and CVE-2026-20184 lets anyone impersonate Webex users without authentication.
item.content:encoded:
Three CVSS 9.9 scores in one advisory. Cisco's patch release this week for Identity Services Engine and Webex is not a routine item. CVSS 9.9 means remote code execution escalating to root with no physical interaction required, and three of the four critical vulnerabilities here reach it.

CVE-2026-20147, CVE-2026-20180, and CVE-2026-20186 all stem from the same root problem: insufficient input validation in the ISE web administration interface. The authentication bar is low. An attacker needs valid ISE credentials, but read-only administrative access is enough — the kind of access a compromised help desk account or a disgruntled contractor would hold. From there, a crafted HTTP request reaches the ISE node, code runs, and the attacker escalates to root on the underlying OS. Cisco's advisory confirms the escalation path.

Why that matters specifically: Cisco ISE is the network access control backbone for most large enterprise environments. It handles 802.1X authentication for every wired and wireless endpoint. Root on ISE means an attacker can manipulate which devices are allowed onto the network, issue certificates, intercept authentication flows, and pivot anywhere in the environment. Shodan queries shared by researchers show around 812 ISE appliances currently internet-exposed.

CVE-2026-20184 in Webex is a separate flaw rated CVSS 9.8. It affects how the SSO integration validates certificates against Cisco's Control Hub. An unauthenticated remote attacker can impersonate any user in a Webex deployment. Cisco has patched its cloud infrastructure, but organizations using SSO must manually upload a new identity provider SAML certificate to Control Hub. That step is not automatic. If your Webex deployment uses SSO and you have not done this, user impersonation is open.

Cisco has not confirmed exploitation in the wild. There are no workarounds for any of the four CVEs. Patch versions: ISE 3.1 requires patch 11; ISE 3.2 requires patch 10; ISE 3.3 requires patch 10; ISE 3.4 requires patch 6; ISE 3.5 requires patch 3. The Webex SAML certificate upload procedure is documented in Cisco's advisory for CVE-2026-20184.

item.title: Pierce County Library Breach Exposed Patrons' Social Security Numbers. Ask Why a Library Had Them.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The disclosed breach window is April 15–21. Names, dates of birth, SSNs, and financial information were compromised. The real question is the data model.
item.content:encoded:
Pierce County Library System in Washington disclosed this week that an intrusion between April 15 and April 21 exposed patron records including names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, and financial information. The library has started notifying affected patrons and offering credit monitoring.

A regional library getting breached isn't, by itself, remarkable. The part worth pausing on is what was in the database to begin with.

Library systems in the US historically collected very little on patrons — a card number, a name, maybe an address. The SSN-and-financial-info part crept in over the last decade as libraries started offering adjacent services: online account self-service, device lending, interlibrary loan with collections on damaged items, payment processing for fines and passport acceptance. Each expansion added a field. Nobody ever sat down and asked whether a library card holder's SSN should be retrievable by a compromised admin account two years after they last checked out a book.

That's the pattern you see across local-government breaches in 2026 generally: not a failure of the perimeter, but a failure of data minimization. Retain less, expose less. It's the one piece of advice that would have changed the blast radius here.

If you're a Pierce County patron, the practical move is the usual one: freeze your credit at all three bureaus, enroll in the monitoring the library is offering, and watch for targeted phishing that name-drops the library to establish familiarity. Attackers know exactly which data they stole.

item.title: Vercel's Breach Came Through a Third-Party AI Tool an Employee Clicked 'Allow All' On
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A Vercel staffer's broad OAuth grant to Context.ai gave attackers a path from a March AWS compromise into customer environment variables, exposing API keys for crypto and fintech developers.
item.content:encoded:
One employee's 'Allow All' button. That is the entry point. On April 20th, Vercel disclosed that an attacker had accessed customer environment variables by chaining through Context.ai, a third-party AI productivity tool used internally, which had itself been breached in March via unauthorized access to its AWS environment.

The attack chain is worth walking through because it reflects a pattern that will keep repeating. Context.ai offers an AI office suite that connects to Google Workspace. At least one Vercel employee authorized it using their corporate account with maximum OAuth scope. When attackers compromised Context.ai's infrastructure and obtained its stored OAuth tokens, that broad grant translated directly into control of the employee's Vercel Google Workspace account. From there, attackers pivoted into Vercel's internal environments and pulled project environment variables not flagged as 'sensitive' in the platform.

Vercel's architecture separates sensitive-flagged variables into an encrypted store the attackers did not reach. What lived in the unsecured store: the things developers put into CI/CD pipelines assuming internal-only access — third-party API keys, database connection strings, service credentials. Crypto and fintech developers building on Vercel reported scrambling to rotate keys the same afternoon of disclosure. CoinDesk tracked the fallout in real time as developers cycled through their infrastructure looking for exposure.

ShinyHunters posted a claim on BreachForums asking $2 million for the stolen data, then told BleepingComputer the group had nothing to do with it. Infostealers.com separately reported that the Context.ai breach originated from an infostealer infection at the company, meaning the attacker likely bought stolen credentials from a stealer log rather than breaking into Context.ai's systems directly. Vercel says the investigation is ongoing.

The scope here extends well beyond Vercel. Context.ai serves hundreds of organizations. Any company whose employees authorized it with Google Workspace admin-level scope during the window of the March compromise is a potential victim of the same attack chain. Context.ai is one of thousands of AI productivity tools that have made 'connect your workspace' a core product feature, typically requesting the widest OAuth scopes the consent screen allows.

Review your Google Workspace connected apps today. Pull the OAuth scope list, revoke anything with admin-level access that IT did not explicitly approve, and rotate credentials for any service whose keys might have lived in Vercel project settings. Going forward, treat every AI tool OAuth grant as a third-party vendor security review, not a convenience checkbox.

item.title: GPT-5 Is Here and It's the First Model That Feels Genuinely Multimodal
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI's new flagship handles text, vision, audio, and code in one pass. The benchmarks are impressive. The deployment timeline is aggressive.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI shipped GPT-5 this morning. The short version: one model, four modalities, and the closest thing we've seen to a system that actually reasons across them instead of stitching specialists together behind an API.

The benchmark numbers OpenAI disclosed are what you'd expect — nearly 90% on MMLU, more than doubling GPT-4's score on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. Worth noting that MMLU is increasingly saturated as a test, so the real question is whether the jump shows up in the kind of messy, ambiguous work people actually want models to do.

Early reads suggest it does. The tasks OpenAI is emphasizing in its rollout materials are agentic ones: multi-step engineering work, research that spans dozens of sources, tool use across APIs without human checkpoints in the middle. If that holds up in the wild, it's the capability leap that matters more than any benchmark score.

The industry response was fast. Anthropic and Google DeepMind both have competing releases queued, and the calendar just got pulled forward. Nvidia traded up on the assumption that training and inference demand just got bigger.

Access is tiered. ChatGPT Enterprise customers and Tier-1 API partners get the first 30 days. Safety researchers at the Alignment Forum have already pushed back on the pace, arguing red-team evaluations on a model this capable warrant more than the compressed window OpenAI ran. OpenAI hasn't adjusted the schedule.

item.title: Russia's APT29 Is Burning a Windows Zero-Day Across NATO Government Networks
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-21954 is an NTLM relay flaw with a CVSS of 9.8. Microsoft just patched it. CISA gave federal agencies 48 hours.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft's Threat Intelligence Center confirmed this morning what incident responders at CrowdStrike and Mandiant had been piecing together for two weeks: APT29, the Russian SVR group also tracked as Midnight Blizzard, has been quietly burning a Windows NTLM zero-day across NATO government networks.

The bug, now CVE-2026-21954, lets an unauthenticated attacker relay NTLM credentials to domain-level persistence without user interaction. Every supported version of Windows Server from 2016 through 2025 is vulnerable, along with every default-configured Windows 10 and 11 endpoint. That's most of the enterprise install base.

Initial access was spearphishing — emails crafted to look like NATO internal communications. Once a single workstation clicked through, responders say the group was at domain admin in an average of seven minutes. That's fast enough that human detection is not realistic; you're relying on your EDR to catch it.

CISA issued Emergency Directive ED-26-03 giving federal civilian agencies 48 hours to apply Microsoft's out-of-band patch. The directive also requires domain controller segmentation and, where operationally feasible, disabling NTLM outright. That second ask will land hard at agencies with legacy dependencies.

At least 14 NATO-affiliated agencies across Eastern Europe have confirmed compromise. Three intelligence services were notified privately through the Shadowserver Foundation. If you manage a Windows environment, assume exposure until you can prove otherwise: audit NTLM authentication logs for the past 30 days, patch immediately, and review any domain admin logons that don't map to known activity.

item.title: Starship Caught Both Stages on the Same Flight. That's Never Been Done.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SpaceX pulled off a double tower catch at Starbase this morning after a full 90-minute orbital mission. Watch the footage. It looks fake.
item.content:encoded:
Early Thursday at Starbase, the Super Heavy booster came back first — caught by the Mechazilla tower arms the way it has been three times before. Then Starship came home. Relit its Raptors on a trajectory nobody was expecting, flew back, and let the same tower catch it too. Both stages. Same mission.

No orbital vehicle has ever been fully recovered before. Not even close. The Shuttle orbiter landed like a glider and the boosters splashed down. Falcon 9 boosters land, but the second stage is expendable. What SpaceX did this morning changes the cost curve of getting to orbit by an order of magnitude, assuming they can do it twice.

The flight itself ran 90 minutes. Apogee at 310 km. Sixty Starlink V3 satellites deployed on the first pass, which is almost incidental at this point. The Raptor relight for the return was the part nobody outside SpaceX was told about in advance.

NASA cares about this in a specific way: the Artemis III lunar landing hinges on Starship delivering crew to the Moon's surface by 2028, and every flight that demonstrates reuse and reliability is a flight that makes that schedule plausible.

SpaceX says the next Starship flight is 45 days out. The objective is in-orbit propellant transfer, the technology that makes everything beyond low Earth orbit possible with this vehicle. If they pull that off too, the next decade of space is going to look very different from the last one.

item.title: Google's Willow Chip Just Cleared the Biggest Hurdle in Quantum Computing
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Adding more qubits is supposed to make error rates worse. On Willow, it makes them exponentially better. That's the threshold the field has been chasing for 30 years.
item.content:encoded:
Google announced today that its 105-qubit Willow processor has crossed the error-correction threshold, meaning that when they add more physical qubits to a logical qubit, the error rate drops exponentially instead of climbing. That sentence is unremarkable until you realize it's the single hurdle that has stood between noisy-intermediate-scale quantum machines and actually-useful quantum machines for three decades.

For proof-of-work, Willow ran a random circuit sampling benchmark in under five minutes. The classical supercomputer equivalent is a number so large it stops having meaning — Google cites 10 septillion years. Take the specific figure with a grain of salt (it's sensitive to which classical algorithm you compare against), but the order of magnitude is real.

Hartmut Neven, who leads Quantum AI at Google, was deliberately cautious about application timelines. Willow is not factoring RSA-2048 next year. What it does is remove the biggest open scientific question from the path. Engineering a commercial quantum computer is now an engineering problem, not a physics problem.

That's a meaningful distinction for cryptography. The security community has been talking about post-quantum migration on the theory that capable quantum machines are maybe 10 or 15 years out. Willow doesn't shorten that window by itself, but it confirms the window is closing, and organizations sitting on 15-year-sensitive data should be accelerating, not waiting.

IBM and Microsoft responded with their own timelines. IBM is targeting its error-threshold milestone by end of year using a different architecture; Microsoft continues to bet on topological qubits. Three companies, three approaches, all suddenly credible. The race is on.

item.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Is Now Live: What's New and What Changed
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The latest Security+ exam overhauls the domain structure with heavier emphasis on cloud security, zero-trust architecture, and AI-assisted threat detection.
item.content:encoded:
CompTIA officially retired the SY0-601 version of Security+ on July 31, 2024 and has been running SY0-701 as the sole active exam since then. The new version reflects a substantially updated threat environment — candidates who studied for the old exam will find significant differences in both content and question style.

The most notable structural change is a reduction from six domains to five. The new domains are: General Security Concepts (12%), Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%), Security Architecture (18%), Security Operations (28%), and Security Program Management and Oversight (20%). The weighting signals that CompTIA views hands-on operational skills as increasingly central to the certification's value.

Cloud security now permeates the entire exam rather than sitting in an isolated domain. Candidates must understand shared responsibility models, cloud-native security controls, serverless and container security, and CASB deployment — all areas that were lightly covered in SY0-601. Zero-trust architecture (ZTA) is explicitly examined for the first time, including microsegmentation, identity-centric access, and continuous verification principles.

A new focus on AI and automation has been added. Candidates need to understand how machine learning is applied to SIEM correlation, endpoint detection and response (EDR), and user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA). This does not require deep AI expertise but does expect familiarity with how these tools function in a modern SOC.

For study resources, CompTIA's own CertMaster Learn and CertMaster Labs remain the most closely aligned materials. Professor Messer's free SY0-701 video series has been widely praised as the best no-cost option. Jason Dion's Udemy course and Mike Chapple's official CompTIA study guide (Sybex) are the top-rated paid options. Most candidates report needing 60–90 days of dedicated study for a first attempt.

item.title: Scattered Spider Locked Up 47 Hospitals Over a Weekend. A Phone Call Started It.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: One vishing call to an IT help desk was enough to unwind MFA on an admin account. Eight petabytes encrypted. Ambulances diverted in Phoenix for six hours.
item.content:encoded:
The initial access was a phone call. Someone impersonating an IT help desk vendor got an admin at one of three regional health networks to reset MFA on a privileged account. An hour later, Scattered Spider was inside; by the end of the weekend, 47 hospitals across six states were running on paper.

The payload was Black Cat (ALPHV). The group used the organization's own remote access tooling to move laterally — the kind of living-off-the-land tradecraft that makes EDR detection hard even when it's working properly. Eight petabytes of patient data and backups were encrypted before anyone realized what was happening.

The ransom demand is $50 million in Monero. The FBI, CISA, and HHS are coordinating the response. Affected hospitals are using paper-based emergency procedures designed for natural disasters, not for weeks of sustained outage.

The human cost is already real. Three patients had elective surgeries cancelled inside their pre-op window. Two hospitals in Phoenix diverted incoming ambulances for six hours. Claroty estimates total disruption will exceed $750 million when recovery, downtime, and regulatory exposure are added up.

Senator Mark Warner's Critical Infrastructure Resilience Act, which would require hospitals to maintain offline backups, has been stalled for two years by industry lobbying. It's expected to get a Senate floor vote next month. If it doesn't pass after this, it's fair to ask what would have to happen for it to pass.
